title: Plan B and Alcohol: Can You Drink? Timing and Vomiting Rules
excerpt: Can you take Plan B after drinking? Why alcohol doesn't interact with the pill, what to do if you throw up, how timing matters, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you take Plan B and drink alcohol? Alcohol doesn't stop it working, but vomiting and delays can. What to do if you throw up, and timing rules.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, you can take Plan B if you've been drinking, and drinking after you take it won't stop it from working. There is no known chemical interaction between alcohol and levonorgestrel, the hormone in Plan B One-Step and its generic versions. The real risks are indirect: **throwing up soon after taking the pill**, and **waiting too long** because you were drunk, hungover, or asleep. Both of those can matter more than the alcohol itself. This guide explains why, what to do if you vomit, and how to handle the timing after a night out.

**The quick rules:** Take Plan B as soon as you can. Don't wait until you've sobered up or the hangover has passed, because it works best the sooner it's taken. If you feel queasy, eat something light first and sip water. If you vomit within about two to three hours of taking it, contact a pharmacist or doctor about taking another dose. Drinking afterward is fine as far as the pill is concerned, but heavy drinking that makes you sick in that window is the thing to avoid.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a pharmacist, doctor, or sexual health clinic that knows your situation. **Talk to a pharmacist or doctor if** you vomited within a few hours of taking emergency contraception, you take any other medicines (especially seizure medicines, certain HIV or tuberculosis drugs, or St. John's wort), it has been more than three days since unprotected sex, or you aren't sure which option is right for you. **Seek urgent care** for severe stomach pain, fainting, or signs of alcohol poisoning such as confusion, repeated vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, or being hard to wake. In an emergency, call 911.

## Does Alcohol Make Plan B Less Effective?

No. There's no good evidence that alcohol reduces how well Plan B works, and the official product information doesn't list alcohol as an interaction. Here's why that makes sense.

Plan B contains a single 1.5 mg dose of **levonorgestrel**, a synthetic version of the hormone progesterone. Its main job is to **delay or prevent ovulation**, meaning it stops an ovary from releasing an egg for a few days, so sperm that are already present don't meet one. It doesn't work once ovulation has already happened, which is one reason timing matters so much.

Your liver breaks levonorgestrel down mainly with an enzyme called **CYP3A4**. The medicines known to weaken emergency contraception are ones that speed up that enzyme, which doctors call "enzyme inducers." Examples include the antibiotic rifampin, some seizure medicines such as carbamazepine and phenytoin, some HIV medicines, and the herbal supplement St. John's wort. These make the body clear the hormone faster, so less of it is around to do its job.

Alcohol isn't in that group. A night of drinking doesn't meaningfully speed up how fast your liver clears levonorgestrel, and alcohol doesn't block the hormone from being absorbed. So the pill itself is unaffected whether you drink before it, after it, or both.

That's the pharmacology. The practical picture has a few more moving parts, and they're covered below.

## Can You Take Plan B While Drunk or Hungover?

Yes. You don't need to wait until you're sober, and you shouldn't. Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so the best time to take it is as soon as you reasonably can after unprotected sex or a contraceptive failure (a broken condom, missed pills, and so on).

A few things to keep in mind if you're still drunk or hungover:

- **Read the box once, carefully.** It's one tablet, swallowed with water. You don't need to take anything else with it. If you're not sure you've taken it, check the blister pack before considering another dose.
- **Eat something light if your stomach is unsettled.** Plan B can be taken with or without food. A few crackers or some toast can make nausea less likely, and nausea is the thing you're trying to avoid.
- **Sip water rather than gulping.** Drinking a large amount quickly on an upset stomach is a common trigger for vomiting.
- **Don't take anti-nausea or other medicines you wouldn't normally use** without checking with a pharmacist. Most common hangover remedies don't interact with levonorgestrel, but it's worth a quick check if you're unsure.

If you're too drunk to make a clear decision or get to a pharmacy safely, it's reasonable to rest and get it first thing in the morning. Plan B is labeled for use within 72 hours, so a few hours' delay to stay safe isn't the end of the line. Just don't let the hangover push it to the next day or the day after.

## Is It Safe to Drink After Taking Plan B?

As far as the pill goes, yes. Having a drink after you've taken Plan B won't undo it. Once the hormone is absorbed, it's doing its work regardless of what you drink next.

The one caveat is vomiting. The pill needs a couple of hours to be absorbed. If you drink enough in that window to make yourself sick, you may lose some or all of the dose. So the sensible approach is:

- **Give it a few hours before drinking heavily.** A drink with dinner is not a problem. A big night out right after taking it is where the vomiting risk comes in.
- **If you're already feeling sick from drinking, hold off on more alcohol** until you're sure the pill has stayed down for a few hours.

There's also a second reason to go easy for a day or two. Plan B's own side effects (nausea, headache, tiredness, dizziness, cramps) overlap almost exactly with hangover symptoms. Stacking a hangover on top of them can make you feel considerably worse, and it makes it harder to tell what's causing what.

## What If You Throw Up After Taking Plan B?

This is the most important section of this guide, because vomiting is the one realistic way alcohol can cause Plan B to fail.

The guidance depends on how long after the pill you were sick:

| When you vomited | What it generally means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Within about 2 hours of taking Plan B | The pill may not have been fully absorbed | Contact a pharmacist or doctor promptly. You may need another dose. |
| 2 to 3 hours after | Gray zone. Some guidance (including UK sexual health guidance) uses a 3-hour cut-off | Contact a pharmacist or doctor to ask whether to repeat the dose. |
| More than 3 hours after | The hormone is generally considered absorbed | No repeat dose is usually needed. |

The US Plan B One-Step label tells people to call a healthcare professional if they vomit within two hours of taking it. UK guidance from the Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare uses a three-hour window for repeating a levonorgestrel dose. The exact figure varies a bit by source, which is why the practical advice is simple: **if you were sick within a few hours, ask a professional rather than guess.**

A few practical points if this happens:

- **Note the time you took the pill and the time you were sick.** A pharmacist will ask for both.
- **Don't take a second dose on your own while you're still actively vomiting.** It's likely to come back up too. Ask about anti-nausea options and timing.
- **A pharmacist can often help the same day.** In many places Plan B is sold over the counter without age or ID requirements, and pharmacists are used to this question.
- **Ask about other options.** If keeping a pill down is a problem, a copper IUD inserted by a clinician is another form of emergency contraception that doesn't depend on absorbing a pill at all. It's also considered the most effective option.

If you're vomiting repeatedly, can't keep water down, or are very drunk, that's a separate concern from contraception. See the "when to get help" section below.

## Timing Matters More Than Alcohol

If there's one thing alcohol genuinely threatens, it's timing. A heavy night can lead to:

- Not noticing a condom broke, or not remembering whether one was used
- Forgetting a regular birth control pill, which can create the need for emergency contraception in the first place
- Sleeping late, feeling too rough to go out, and putting off the pharmacy trip

Here's why that matters. Plan B is labeled for use within **72 hours (3 days)** of unprotected sex, and it works best the sooner it's taken. Because its main action is delaying ovulation, every hour you wait is an hour in which ovulation might happen first. Once an egg has been released, levonorgestrel can't stop it.

Your options also depend on how much time has passed:

- **Levonorgestrel pills (Plan B and generics):** labeled for up to 72 hours, best taken as early as possible. Some guidance notes it may still have some effect up to 5 days, but it's less reliable later.
- **Ulipristal acetate (sold as ella in the US, ellaOne in the UK and Europe):** works for up to 5 days (120 hours) and holds its effectiveness better across that window than levonorgestrel. In the US it needs a prescription, which many telehealth services and some pharmacists can provide quickly.
- **Copper IUD:** can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sex and is the most effective form of emergency contraception. It also gives ongoing contraception afterward.

There's no good evidence that alcohol interacts with ulipristal either, and the same vomiting rule applies: UK guidance recommends a repeat dose if you're sick within three hours.

So if you're reading this the morning after, the most useful thing you can do isn't to worry about the drinks you had. It's to get emergency contraception today.

## Plan B Side Effects vs Hangover Symptoms

Plan B is generally well tolerated, but it does have side effects, and many of them look like a hangover. Here's how they compare:

| Symptom | Common with Plan B? | Common with a hangover? |
|---|---|---|
| Nausea | Yes | Yes |
| Vomiting | Less common | Yes, after heavy drinking |
| Headache | Yes | Yes |
| Tiredness | Yes | Yes |
| Dizziness | Yes | Yes |
| Lower stomach cramps | Yes | Sometimes |
| Breast tenderness | Yes | No |
| Irregular spotting or a changed period | Yes | No |

The overlap is why the combination can feel rough. It's also why it's worth paying attention to symptoms that don't fit either pattern, such as severe or one-sided stomach pain. That's covered in the warning signs below.

Most Plan B side effects fade within a day or two. Your next period may come a little early or late. The label advises taking a pregnancy test if your period is more than a week late.

For easing the hangover side, the basics help: water, a light meal, rest, and time. Our guide on [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has practical tips for settling your stomach, which is doubly useful when you need a pill to stay down.

## Can You Take Hangover Medicines With Plan B?

Generally, the common over-the-counter hangover helpers don't interact with levonorgestrel. That includes ibuprofen, acetaminophen, antacids, and electrolyte drinks. A few cautions still apply, but they're about the alcohol, not the Plan B:

- **Ibuprofen and aspirin** can irritate a stomach that's already upset from drinking. Take them with food. See our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is hard on the liver in large doses after drinking. Stick to one standard dose. Our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide explains why.
- **Antacids** like Tums are fine to use for heartburn. If you're worried about anything affecting absorption, leave a gap of a couple of hours after the pill.
- **Herbal supplements:** St. John's wort is the one to watch. It speeds up the enzyme that breaks down levonorgestrel and can make emergency contraception less effective. If you take it regularly, tell the pharmacist, because a different dose or option may be recommended.

If you take any prescription medicine, especially for seizures, HIV, or tuberculosis, mention it to the pharmacist. Those are the medicines that genuinely affect emergency contraception, far more than anything you drank. For a wider view of how common medicines and supplements interact, see our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Other Things That Affect How Well Plan B Works

Since alcohol isn't really the issue, it's worth knowing what is. Beyond timing, vomiting, and interacting medicines, the main one discussed in the research is body weight.

Some studies have suggested levonorgestrel emergency contraception may be less effective in people with a higher body weight or BMI. The evidence is mixed. UK guidance suggests a double dose of levonorgestrel or choosing ulipristal or a copper IUD for people above certain weight or BMI thresholds, while the FDA has said the data are not consistent enough to change the US label. If this applies to you, it's a good question to raise with a pharmacist or doctor, who can talk through which option suits you best.

None of these factors are made better or worse by having a few drinks.

## Does Alcohol Affect Regular Birth Control Pills?

This is a related question many people have, so it's worth a short answer. Like Plan B, regular birth control pills don't have a known chemical interaction with alcohol. Drinking doesn't make them stop working.

The risks are the same indirect ones:

- **Vomiting soon after a pill.** For most combined pills, being sick within about two to three hours of taking one can mean it wasn't absorbed. Check your pill's leaflet, which will say what counts as a missed pill and what to do.
- **Forgetting a pill** because of a late night, a disrupted routine, or a bad hangover. Progestogen-only "mini pills" can have a strict time window, so a late pill matters more with them.

If either happens, the pill's leaflet or a pharmacist can tell you whether you need backup contraception or emergency contraception. Setting a phone alarm for your pill is a simple fix that holds up well on nights out.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who take Plan B after drinking will have a rough morning at worst. But some symptoms need prompt attention, and it's important not to dismiss them as "just a hangover."

**Contact a pharmacist or doctor soon if:**

- You vomited within about two to three hours of taking Plan B
- You take seizure medicines, certain HIV or tuberculosis medicines, or St. John's wort
- It has been more than 72 hours since unprotected sex, or you aren't sure of the timing
- Your period is more than a week late after taking Plan B

**Seek urgent medical care if:**

- You have **severe lower stomach pain**, especially on one side, in the weeks after taking Plan B. The label advises seeing a doctor promptly for this.
- You feel faint, dizzy enough to fall, or have unusual heavy bleeding
- Someone shows signs of **alcohol poisoning**: confusion, vomiting that won't stop, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, or being hard to wake

Alcohol poisoning is a medical emergency. Call 911 (or your local emergency number), keep the person on their side, and don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." This applies regardless of any medicine they've taken.

If vomiting after a night out keeps happening, can't be controlled, or comes with severe stomach pain, that's a reason to see a doctor in its own right.

## A Practical Morning-After Checklist

If you're reading this after a night of drinking and you need emergency contraception, here's the short version of what to do:

1. **Get emergency contraception today.** Don't wait for the hangover to pass. Earlier is better.
2. **Eat something light and sip water** before and after taking the pill to lower the chance of nausea.
3. **Note the time you take it.**
4. **Avoid more alcohol for a few hours**, and go easy for the rest of the day.
5. **If you're sick within about two to three hours, call a pharmacist or doctor** about a repeat dose or another option.
6. **Mention any other medicines you take** to the pharmacist, especially seizure, HIV, or tuberculosis medicines, or St. John's wort.
7. **Rest and rehydrate.** Side effects and hangover symptoms usually fade within a day or two.

## Making Nights Out Easier on Your Body

None of this needs much more than common sense, but there's a pattern worth noticing. The main way alcohol interferes with contraception is by making you sick or making you forget. Drinking at a steadier pace, eating beforehand, and alternating with water all make vomiting less likely and keep you clearer-headed. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains how fast your body actually clears it.

Some people also use supplements to make the morning after easier. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited data in people, so it's best thought of as promising rather than settled. There's no known interaction between DHM and levonorgestrel, but there's also no research on taking them together, so if you'd like to use both, run it past a pharmacist. DHM does not affect whether Plan B works, and it's no substitute for taking emergency contraception promptly. If you're curious, a straightforward single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular combination formula. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol doesn't interact with Plan B, and there's no good evidence that drinking makes it less effective.
- You can take Plan B while drunk or hungover. Don't delay it to sober up, because it works best the sooner it's taken.
- The real risk from drinking is **vomiting within about two to three hours** of the pill. If that happens, contact a pharmacist or doctor about a repeat dose.
- Timing matters most: Plan B is labeled for up to 72 hours. Ulipristal (ella) and a copper IUD work for up to 5 days.
- Medicines like certain seizure drugs and St. John's wort can weaken emergency contraception. Alcohol doesn't.
- Severe stomach pain after taking Plan B, or signs of alcohol poisoning, need urgent medical care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take Plan B and drink alcohol?**

Yes. There's no known interaction between alcohol and levonorgestrel, the hormone in Plan B, and the product information doesn't list alcohol as a concern. The main thing to avoid is drinking so much in the first few hours after taking it that you vomit, because that can stop the pill from being absorbed.

**Does alcohol make Plan B less effective?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Plan B is broken down by a liver enzyme called CYP3A4, and the medicines that weaken it are ones that speed up that enzyme, such as some seizure medicines, certain HIV and tuberculosis drugs, and St. John's wort. Alcohol isn't one of them. Indirectly, alcohol can cause problems by making you vomit or by delaying when you take the pill.

**Can I take Plan B while drunk?**

Yes, and it's better not to wait until you're sober, because emergency contraception works best the sooner it's taken. Eat something light and sip water to reduce the chance of nausea. If you're too drunk to get to a pharmacy safely, getting it first thing the next morning is reasonable, since Plan B is labeled for use within 72 hours.

**How long after taking Plan B can I drink?**

The pill itself isn't affected by alcohol, so there's no strict waiting period. Because the hormone needs a couple of hours to be absorbed, it's sensible to avoid heavy drinking for at least a few hours afterward so you don't risk vomiting it back up. A single drink with a meal isn't a concern.

**What should I do if I threw up after taking Plan B?**

If you vomited within about two hours of taking it (some guidance, including UK guidance, uses three hours), contact a pharmacist or doctor promptly. You may need another dose. If it was more than three hours later, the hormone is generally considered absorbed and a repeat dose usually isn't needed. Note the times you took the pill and were sick, as a pharmacist will ask.

**Do Plan B side effects feel like a hangover?**

They can. Common Plan B side effects include nausea, headache, tiredness, dizziness, and lower stomach cramps, which overlap heavily with hangover symptoms. Breast tenderness and changes to your next period are side effects of the pill rather than alcohol. Severe or one-sided stomach pain is not a normal side effect of either and needs prompt medical attention.

**Can I take ibuprofen or Tylenol with Plan B after drinking?**

These common pain relievers don't interact with levonorgestrel. The usual alcohol cautions still apply: take ibuprofen with food to protect your stomach, and keep acetaminophen to a single standard dose after drinking to go easy on your liver. If you take St. John's wort or prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist, as some of those can affect emergency contraception.

**Does alcohol affect ella (ulipristal) emergency contraception?**

There's no known interaction between alcohol and ulipristal acetate either. The same vomiting rule applies: UK guidance recommends a repeat dose if you're sick within three hours of taking it. Ulipristal works for up to 5 days after unprotected sex and needs a prescription in the US.
